entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240 – 1313), a polymath of Catalan origin, stood as one of the most influential intellectual figures of the late medieval period, bridging the worlds of medicine, alchemy, and theology. Born near Valencia or Mallorca, his intellectual journey spanned major European centers, from the burgeoning medical schools of Montpellier to the papal courts of Rome and Avignon. He gained renown as a physician to kings and popes, including Peter III of Aragon, Frederick II of Sicily, and Popes Boniface VIII and Clement V, making him a central figure in the intellectual and political landscape of the Mediterranean world.

His core contributions lie in his extensive medical writings, which synthesized classical Greek and Arabic traditions with his own clinical observations. Works like *Speculum Medicinae* and *Breviarium Practicae* became standard texts, influencing medical curricula for centuries. Beyond medicine, Arnaldus was a significant alchemist, whose writings such as *Rosarium Philosophorum* explored the transmutation of metals and the preparation of elixirs, contributing to the development of early chemistry. He was also a fervent religious reformer, deeply immersed in Joachite apocalypticism, predicting the imminent arrival of the Antichrist and advocating for radical ecclesiastical reform, which often brought him into conflict with the established Church.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Arnaldus de Villa Nova significantly advanced medieval medical practice and pharmacology through his influential writings, while also impacting religious thought with his apocalyptic prophecies, shaping both scientific and spiritual discourse across Europe.
